segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Phoebe Langton came down the staircase of Amberlight House first, and found Mrs Pike in the hall below with one hand already laid on the newel post.

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: My dear, the door was open to the lane. Where is the chain?

segments.speaker: Miss Phoebe Langton
segments.text: There is no chain, ma'am. There is a trunk with a handle come away, and a young lady who fainted picking up her letters.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Harker had come down behind her. He stopped three steps up and spoke over Phoebe's head to both women at once.

segments.speaker: Mr Edward Harker
segments.text: Miss Fairfax was to have been married in June. Her intended's mother said in a room full of people that she had gone after a dead man's money, and the thing was broken off in April. She came here to be out of the way of faces that knew her. You may carry that down the lane with my name at the end of it.

segments.speaker: Mrs Hale
segments.text: Well. That is a wicked thing for a mother to say.

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: It is, and I never once said madness. Grief, I said. I said to Mrs Hale only on Saturday that there was a sorrow in that house, and a sorrow is a very different article.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Mrs Hale pushed her spectacles up into her hair and said nothing whatever. Mrs Pike had already turned, and was looking from Harker on the stair to Phoebe at the foot of it.

segments.speaker: Mrs Honoria Pike
segments.text: A gentleman who settles a young woman's account at the draper's and will not put his name to it is not being mean, my dear. I shall say no more than that. But I shall expect to hear something by Lady Day.

segments.speaker: Mrs Hale
segments.text: I shall repeat it exactly as I had it, ma'am.

segments.speaker: Miss Phoebe Langton
segments.text: Then repeat the one pound eleven with it, and say it was owed.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: On Monday morning Augusta Fairfax crossed the yard in black bombazine cut to her own measure, taken standing up, on the Saturday. Mr Rowe held the schoolroom door for her and talked the whole way, as he does.

segments.speaker: Mr Silas Rowe
segments.text: The stove smokes when the wind is in the east, which it is, and the little ones read very badly and very loudly. I say that so you are not disappointed in them.

segments.speaker: Miss Augusta Fairfax
segments.text: I should like to hear the youngest, if you will have me. I am not fit for much else yet.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Ludd boy, who had put his ear to that wall and heard her crying through it, read four lines to her about a ship and got two of them right.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: By dusk Phoebe was walking down the lane with Harker beside her, because he had said he would see her to the green and she had not troubled to argue it.

segments.speaker: Mr Edward Harker
segments.text: I gave you a worn poplin gown and told you to manage. I have thought of it every day since.

segments.speaker: Miss Phoebe Langton
segments.text: And I stood in the lane counting your money and decided you had bought my silence with it. We were both wrong in the same hall, sir, within the same five minutes.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At the turn of the lane she looked back. The shutters were off the main block, and there was a candle in every window of it, and the east wing was lit too, where Mr Rowe was locking up by the one he could least afford to burn.

segments.speaker: Mr Edward Harker
segments.text: Send your bill up to the house for Miss Fairfax's mourning. Put your name to it, and I shall put mine under it.
